opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that it made me take the more "naive" extrapolation-style models a bit more seriously than I would have otherwise, while also making me more aware of what they leave out.

When we first put out the time-horizon work, measuring the length of tasks, in terms of how long they take skilled humans, that models can complete with some reliability, my prior was that a clean exponential trend like that would probably be fragile. You'd expect that if you changed the task distribution, or the success threshold, or the way you estimate human completion time, the slope would move around a lot. And to some extent the absolute numbers do move. If you look at messier tasks, or tasks that are less well specified, the horizons are shorter. But the doubling time has been surprisingly stable across a lot of those choices. That's the part that surprised me.

On economic models specifically, a lot of the models people build, whether it's task-based automation models or the more compute-centric takeoff models, have this structure where you're mapping inputs like compute, algorithmic progress, and labor onto some notion of capabilities, and then mapping capabilities onto economic impact. The second mapping has always been the really hand-wavy part. People basically guess at what fraction of tasks gets automated as a function of effective compute. Time horizon gives you something a bit more grounded to put in the middle. It's still a proxy, but it's in units that at least gesture at economically meaningful work, which is how long a person would take to do it.

So the robustness made me think there might be a fairly stable relationship between inputs and this one capability measure, and that's useful for anchoring. But I want to be careful, because it also clarified where I'm skeptical. Our tasks are mostly self-contained software and research engineering tasks with automatic scoring. Real economic work involves a lot of context, coordination, ambiguity, and long-running feedback loops. So translating "the model can do a four-hour benchmark task at 50% reliability" into "this much of the economy is automatable" is still a huge leap. You also have to think about reliability: 50% success is very different from the 99%-plus you'd need for a lot of deployment.

So net, I'd say it pushed me toward thinking trend extrapolation is less crazy than I assumed, and that economic models should probably incorporate something like time horizon as an intermediate variable. But it also made me more insistent that the hard empirical work is in the capabilities-to-impact link, and we shouldn't let a clean line on a log plot convince us we understand that part.

r002.rationale: It says the trend suggests a fairly stable relationship between inputs and a capability measure, but does not connect aggregate AI progress to systematic dynamics despite contingent decisions by individual labs.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think I came into this with a fairly standard sense that the economic models of AI progress—the Epoch-style models, the ones that try to project when you get some kind of explosive growth or when AI starts meaningfully contributing to AI research—were kind of a fun exercise but mostly unconstrained by data. Like, you have these parameters, you can pick reasonable-sounding values, and you get a wide range of outcomes, and it's hard to know which world you're in.

What the time-horizon work did for me is it gave me one concrete, measurable thing that behaves really regularly. When we first put out the trend, I honestly expected it to break. I expected that either the new models wouldn't fit the line, or that we'd find out the task suite was weird in some way that made the trend an artifact. And instead what happened is we kept adding models, we kept adding tasks, we did a bunch of robustness checks—different task distributions, different ways of estimating horizon, looking at it with the success rate thresholds moved around—and the doubling time just stayed in roughly the same range. That's not what you see with a noisy or artifactual metric. That's what you see with something that's actually tracking an underlying capability that's growing in a pretty smooth way.

And so that changed how I think about the economic models in two ways. The first is that it made me take the "inputs" to those models more seriously as things you can actually measure rather than hand-wave about. A lot of the models have some parameter that's basically "how much of the work of a researcher can an AI system do?" and that was historically just a vibe. Now I think time horizon is an imperfect but real proxy for that. If you can do tasks that take a human an hour, you can automate a certain fraction of workflows; if you can do tasks that take a human a week, that's a qualitatively different fraction. So you can start to plug in a trend that's empirical rather than assumed.

The second thing—and this is the one that I think is more uncomfortable—is that the regularity of the trend made me more sympathetic to the fast-takeoff-flavored versions of the models. Not because the trend itself says anything about recursive self-improvement, but because a lot of the skepticism about those models came from the feeling that AI progress is lumpy and unpredictable, so you can't extrapolate. And the time horizon result is kind of a direct piece of evidence against that. Capabilities on this axis have been growing exponentially for several years with a fairly tight doubling time. That doesn't mean it continues, and I want to be really careful here, because extrapolating a trend six years out is a totally different epistemic activity than describing the last six years. But it does mean that the burden of proof shifts a little bit. If you want to say the models are wrong because progress won't be smooth, you now have to explain why this particular smooth thing is going to stop being smooth.

Where I still have a lot of skepticism is in the gap between "can do a task of length X in our benchmark" and "produces economic value in the real world." Our tasks are clean. They have a well-defined success criterion, they don't require coordinating with other people, they don't involve the messy context of an actual job. So I think the time horizon tells you something like an upper bound on capability that the economy then has to figure out how to absorb, and that absorption process is where a lot of the economic models are still basically guessing. But I'd say I went from thinking the models were almost entirely speculative to thinking they have at least one leg standing on real ground, and that's a meaningful shift for me.

r002.rationale: The response says capability growth on this axis has been smooth and regular, but does not connect that systematic progress to contingent decisions by individual labs.

astra-6.text:
It made me put more weight on models where AI progress translates into a fairly steady expansion in the range of tasks that can be automated. If the time horizon over which systems can reliably complete tasks keeps increasing, that gives you a useful connection between improvements in capabilities and potential economic effects.

But I’d distinguish that from saying we’ve established a particular trajectory for economic growth. You still need to know how those tasks fit into actual jobs, how costly it is to deploy the systems, and what bottlenecks remain. So the update is toward taking that kind of model more seriously, while still being quite uncertain about the translation from task performance to economic impact.

sol-6.1.text:
It made me put more weight on models where AI progress translates into a sustained increase in the range of tasks that can be automated. You can look at benchmark improvements and worry that they’re very specific to the benchmark. A trend in the length of tasks models can complete seems closer to something you could actually connect to an economic model.

But I think there’s still a pretty big gap between those two things. Being able to complete a task in an evaluation doesn’t necessarily mean you can economically replace someone doing that task. There are questions about reliability, the amount of supervision you need, and how the task fits into a larger workflow.

So the robustness of the trend updated me more on the technological side of those models than on the whole economic story. It made continued expansion of AI capabilities seem more plausible, but it didn’t by itself establish how quickly that becomes productivity growth or feeds back into faster AI progress.
